thread.title: Logical Problem of the Trinity - LPT
thread.title_full: Logical Problem of the Trinity - LPT

author: Matt Slick
title: Logical Problem of the Trinity - LPT
text:
Many people attack the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, whether they be atheists, Muslims, Unitarians, etc. Sometimes, they present what is called the Logical Problem of the Trinity (LPT). It focuses on the definition of the Trinity where God is one substance (ousia) yet three persons (hypostasis). They argue that it is logically impossible for something to be both one and three in the same respect at the same time. The bring up the idea that the Father, Son, and Spirit are all God, but each is separate from the other. Therefore, there must be three gods, or the Trinity doctrine is illogical. But their criticism is not without a response from the Christian community.
I will reproduce two versions of the so-called logical problem of the Trinity and then respond below.
Logical Problem of the Trinity One God in three distinct, simultaneous, coeternal Persons. Whereas, The Father is God The Son is God The Spirit is God The Father is not the Son The Son is not the Spirit The Spirit is not the Father One Divine Essence Three divine persons If each Person is fully divine/God, and each is not the other, then it follows that there are three Gods, not one—leading to tritheism. If only one God exists, and each Person is not identical to the other, how can each be fully God, yet there still only be one God? There must be three gods (negating that each person is identical to the other) or the Trinity is logically incoherent. Either way, the Trinity is false. LPT stated differently Each person of the Trinity uses “I” uniquely. Three “I’s” imply three minds. Three minds imply three gods. But Trinitarianism asserts there is only one God. Therefore, the Trinity is either a form of tritheism or incoherent.
Response to the Logical Problem of the Trinity There is no logical problem of the Trinity because classical Trinitarian doctrine clarifies what is one and what is three. God is one in essence and three in person, which is not a logical contradiction. Furthermore, when we say the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Spirit is God, we are speaking predicatively. In other words, we are assigning the attribute of the divine to the person of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit. When we say that the Father is not the Son, etc., we’re speaking identically. Let me explain.
The “Is of identity” would be “Clark Kent is Superman.” The “Is a predication” would be “Clark Kent is 6′ 3.” The “Is of identity” is a direct one-to-one correspondence. The “Is of predication” is attributing a characteristic to something. When we understand the difference between the two, there is no logical problem. The “Is of predication” states that the Father, Son, and Spirit all possess properties of true divinity. The “Is of Identity” shows distinction between the persons, not that each person is numerically identical to God.
Time as an illustration Although no analogy is perfect when compared to the Trinity, I propose the idea of time as an illustration of God’s existence, addressing the “Is of predication” and the “Is of identity.”
Time is one thing that is comprised of three aspects: past, present, and future. When we say that the past is time, we are speaking predicatively. We are saying that the past, the present, and the future all process the nature of time. This is the “Is of Predication.” When we say that the past is not the same thing as the present, which is not the same thing as the future, we are speaking in regard to the “Is of Identity.” I other words, the past is not exactly equal in all respects to the present and the future. After all, they are distinct from each other relationally. Yet there is no contradiction.
Applied to the Trinity One God in three distinct, simultaneous, coeternal Persons. Whereas, The Father is God (Predication, possesses divine essence) The Son is God (Predication, possesses divine essence) The Spirit is God (Predication, possesses divine essence) The Father is not the Son (Identity, showing personal distinction) The Son is not the Spirit (Identity, showing personal distinction) The Spirit is not the Father (Identity, showing personal distinction) One Divine Essence (Ontology, no division and no multiplication) Three divine persons (Relationship, eternal distinctions)
The Christian doctrine of the Trinity teaches that God exists as three distinct, simultaneous persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit). Each person possesses a unique relational identity to the other persons (Is of Identity). This means each person is personally distinct and not numerically identical with the others. The Father is not the Son, nor the Spirit. Yet, all three persons share the same undivided divine essence (Is of Predication), meaning that each is fully God by nature. Therefore, God is one single nature (Divine Simplicity) and possesses a unified will (Is of Predication) manifesting through three relationally distinct “I’s” (Is of Identity), emphasizing three personal identities, not three separate minds or gods. All divine attributes (omniscience, omnipresence, etc.) are perfectly one in essence and fully operative in each person (Is of Predication). In this way, the Trinity avoids both tritheism and incoherence: God remains one divine being (Is of Identity) expressed in three persons, where personal distinction (Is of Identity) does not divide the divine essence or indicate separate divinities (Is of Predication)
Stated another way The Christian teaching about the Trinity states there is one God, but this one God is three persons: Father, Son (Jesus), and Holy Spirit. Each person is different from the others relationally. The Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Spirit (Is of Identity). This means each person is a real “someone” with their own identity, not just different ways God acts or appears. But all three persons (Father, Son, and Spirit) fully share everything that makes God (Is of predication). When we say “the Father is God,” “the Son is God,” or “the Spirit is God,” we mean each one truly has the complete nature or qualities of God (Is of Predication). For example, the Father is all-powerful, all-loving, and everywhere present, and so are the Son and the Spirit. That’s the (Is of Predication). Each person “is God” in the sense of having every divine attribute (Is of Predication), but each person is not identical to the other persons (Is of Identity)
